taxonomicNotes: This species from Parque Nacional El Chico in the state of Hidalgo was long assigned to Chiropterotriton multidentatus (Rabb 1958, Wake and Lynch 1976).
This species is part of a unique species complex endemic to Lake Apoyo (Říčan et al. 2016). Changes to the taxonomic concept of this species may warrant reassessment.

Bertola et al. (2018) reported a population related to Phyllurus gulbaru from The Pinnacles, while recognising that this represented an evolutionarily significant unit whose taxonomic status was in need of further investigation. Subsequent morphological and molecular research confirmed that this population should be regarded as a distinct species despite moderately low mtDNA differentiation Hoskin et al. (2019), and these authors accordingly described it as the new species Phyllurus pinnaclensis.

This species was resurrected from the synonymy of Sarcohyla bistincta by Campbell et al. (2018) where it had been placed by Duellman (1964). Additionally, Campbell et al. (2018) synonymised S. calthula and S. ephemera with this species.

Lynch (1976) elevated this taxon to species status with no further comment. Lynch, Ruíz-Carranza and Ardila-Robayo (1994) redescribed the species, and noted a possible synapomorphy with Pristimantis cremnobates.
Genus change from Platymantis to Cornufer (Brown et al. 2015). Adults of this species resemble juveniles of Cornufer papuensis and individuals could be misidentified in the field.

Prior to analysis by Keogh et al. (2008), all Fijian banded iguanas were lumped together as a single species (Brachylophus fasciatus). The Gau Banded Iguana, Brachylophus gau, was newly described in 2017 (Fisher et al. 2017) as being morphologically distinct from the Lau Banded Iguana (Brachylophus fasciatus) and from the Central Fijian Banded Iguana (Brachylophus bulabula).
Molecular analyses suggest close relationship with A. furcatus, A. hellmayri and A. bogotensis, and may form a clade with these species and A. chii, A. correndera and A. antarcticus. Monotypic.
Poodytes albolimbatus (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) was previously listed as Megalurus albolimbatus.
Genus change from Liophryne to Sphenophryne (Rivera et al. 2017).

Previously listed as Megalurulus grosvenori (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) and before that in Cichlornis but reassigned to Cincloramphus following Alström et al. (2018). Until recently treated as conspecific with C. llaneae, C. turipavae and C. whitneyi, but differs from first two in characters given under those species and from C. whitneyi by its broader, longer, blacker mask, encompassing eye and extending to rear ear-coverts (2); longer, thicker tarsus (allow 2); shallower and less curved culmen (1); less graduated tail (1); and dark brown vs black legs (1). Monotypic.

Puffinus newelli (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) has been split into P. newelli and P. myrtae (which see) (Handbook of the Birds of the World and BirdLife International 2018). Martínez-Gómez et al. (2015) found molecular evidence that Newell’s Shearwater Puffinus newelli and Townsend’s Shearwater P. auricularis are conspecific. Although they mention the morphological analysis in del Hoyo and Collar (2014: p386) which gave a Tobias score of 7 to newelli, these authors did not consider the characters in question: larger size (an effect size of 3.29 on tail length yielded a score of 2; new data in Shirihai et al. [2017] yields an effect size of 2.41, thus again a score of 2); cleaner-cut head pattern (score 1); bolder, squarer neck mark (score 2); all-white undertail-coverts (score 2); plus darker upperparts (scored 1 but uncounted).

(These characters and scores are revised below.)

Martínez-Gómez et al. (2015) also mentioned that ‘Howell (2012) proposed a separate treatment based on their differences in morphology, breeding chronology (Ainley et al. 1997; Bourne et al. 1988), and breeding ecology (Spear et al. 1995)’ [NB these citations in quotation marks are not in the reference list below]. Thus it appears that there are behavioural and ecological differences between the taxa in addition to the morphological ones. Martínez-Gómez et al. (2015) cited the case of Charadrius dealbatus as one in which morphological characters are strong but genetic ones non-existent, but they did not mention that del Hoyo and Collar (2014) accepted the morphological characters despite the genetic evidence. In the present case it seems appropriate to continue to consider that two species are involved, pending confirmation of the authors’ molecular work, clarification of the accuracy of the scoring used to maintain the split of newelli in del Hoyo and Collar (2014), and evidence of the behavioural and ecological differences between the taxa.

However, Martínez-Gómez et al. (2015) also found that P. n. myrtae, ‘Rapa Shearwater’, is genetically more distinct from newelli than newelli is from auricularis. On this basis they propose that myrtae be treated as a full species. Such an arrangement is supported by Shirihai et al. (2017), who noted:

Rapa Shearwater is much smaller (in all biometric characters) than the other two taxa…, and is furthermore highly distinctive in having a unique combination of white undertail-coverts (vs. dark in both newelli and auricularis) and whitish inner webs to the remiges, as well as a white face.

There is a contradiction here with del Hoyo and Collar (2014), where the undertail-coverts of newelli, compared to auricularis, are given as ‘white vs white-edged grey’. Further consideration of this point, by examining images online and Plate 16.1 in Howell (2012: 147), indicate that auricularis has marginally more extensive black undertail-coverts than newelli. However, the information contained in Howell (2012) and the references he cited, plus that conveyed in Howell’s Plate 16.1, lead to somewhat differently scored and parsed characters for newelli vs auricularis:  larger size (effect size 2.41 [see above]: 2);  cleaner-cut and blacker head- and neck-sides (2);  more white on undertail-coverts (1); darker upperparts (1); somewhat different feeding ecology, using less upwelled, more stratified waters with more turbulent meteorological features (Spear et al. 1995; allow 1); breeding chronology (Ainley et al. 1997; no score allowed).

By this means newelli continues to achieve species rank under the Tobias criteria. We therefore retain P. newelli as a separate species from P. auricularis until independent genetic analysis supports Martínez-Gómez et al. (2015) and/or until a new full assessment of morphological characters, and of the behavioural/ecological evidence, can be undertaken.

Other Anguilla species have occasionally been stocked in Europe, but none have established a self-sustaining population. Pure A. rostrata (American Eel) have been recorded but are relatively rare (Boëtius 1976). Stocking attempts are likely to have caused this (Frankowski et al. 2008, Marohn et al. 2014). DNA analysis is the best tool to distinguish between the European Eel and other species (e.g. Frankowski et al. 2008), but A. rostrata have fewer vertebrae than A. anguilla (102–112, usually 106–108, vs. 111–119, usually 114–116). Hybrids have been found as larvae in the Sargasso Sea (Als et al. 2011, Pujolar et al. 2014a) and as yellow eels in Iceland where pure A. rostrata and A. anguilla also exist (Albert et al. 2006).
Setophaga flavescens (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) was previously placed in the genus Dendroica following AOU (1998 & supplements).
This species was removed from the synonymy of Craugastor podiciferus by Arias et al. (2019) where it had previously been placed by Taylor (1952).
This is a split from the broader concept of Hemiphractus fasciatus (Hill et al. 2018).
This is a split from the broader concept of Hemiphractus fasciatus (Hill et al. 2018).

Alexandrinus eques (Handbook of the Birds of the World and BirdLife International 2020) was previously listed as Psittacula eques (del Hoyo et al. 2014). Braun et al. (2019) report the situation where the parrot genera Psittinus, Tanygnathus and Mascarinus nest genetically within Psittacula, meaning that either Psittacula replaces these latter three genera or it breaks down into monophyletic genera of their own. The latter course is preferred, building on Braun et al. (2016), where several genera were established, including Alexandrinus for P. krameri, P. eques and P. exsul.

Faivovich and De la Riva (2006), however, continue to recognize it as a valid species, pending a revision of subpopulations associated with the name Hyloscirtus armatus. In the Hyloscirtus armatus group according to Faivovich and De la Riva (2006).

This species is a complex of more than one species.
We follow De la Riva et al. (2000) in considering this species to be separate from Telmatobius marmoratus, and also follow De la Riva (2004) in considering T. jahuira as a synonym of T. verrucosus.

Previously considered to be a subspecies of Telmatobius marmoratus, T. hintoni was elevated to species category by De la Riva (2005) based on morphological and colour differences.

In addition to the holotype, the type series of T. hintoni is comprised of three specimens from Calacoto, La Paz, but these specimens are not conspecific with the holotype, and they were correctly identified as T. marmoratus by Vellard (De la Riva 2005).

This species is distinguished from other similar species by a combination of morphological features and colour patterns (De la Riva 2005). It is possible that the two subpopulations are not conspecific, so further taxonomic studies are needed (I. De la Riva pers. comm. September 2019).

Calidris pygmaea (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Eurynorhynchus as E. pygmeus.

Pelecanoides georgicus has been split into South Georgia Diving-petrel P. georgicus and Whenua Hou Diving-petrel following the application of the Tobias et al. (2010) criteria by Fischer et al. (2018) to a new form of South Georgia Diving-petrel, upon which it emerges as a species on the basis of a score of 8 in comparison with the population of P. georgicus from the South Atlantic Ocean and a score of 9 in comparison with that from the South Indian Ocean. 

There is a technical problem with the authors’ scoring of the two biometric characters, because they could be said to co-vary with the greater size of NZ birds. However, their data indicate that the bill of NZ birds is actually slightly shorter than those of birds from other populations, so the depth could be interpreted as independent of body size and the other character used. The authors appear to have used standard errors rather than standard deviations in their calculations. However, converting SE to SD yields scores of 1 as they indicated. While the scores for plumage differences in the original description are possibly on the generous side, the taxon is clearly valid, but much more study is needed to demonstrate the strength and consistency of the diagnostic characters. With these reservations, its status as a species is nonetheless accepted here.
Sternula lorata (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Sterna.
Callaeas cinereus and C. wilsoni (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as C. cinereus following Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993) and Turbott (1990).
Hypotaenidia owstoni (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Gallirallus.

The subpopulations in Sri Lanka have been assigned to Indosylvirana serendipi and Hydrophylax gracilis (Biju et al. 2014). These species have all been moved from Indosylvirana and Hydrophylax back to Hylarana (Dubois et al. 2021).

This species was previously included in the Oligosoma infrapunctatum species complex but had been recognized as a candidate species by multiple authors, under the informal names Oligosoma aff. infrapunctatum "Chesterfield" (a name properly applied to the sister species Oligosoma salmo) or Oligosomaa aff. infrapunctatum "Alborn".

This taxon, previously included within Oligosoma infrapunctatum, has been informally treated as a part of distinct species by several authors under the name Oligosoma aff. infrapunctatum "southern North Island" (and further split by van Winkel et al. 2018, who restricted its distribution to Hawke's Bay under the name Oligosoma aff. infrapunctatum "Hawke's Bay"). Melzer et al. (2019) formally described this species, coining the name Oligosoma auroraensis later emended to O. aurorarense.

This taxon has previously been included within the O. infrapunctatum species complex, although since its discovery in 1993 it has been recognized as a candidate species under the common name 'Chesterfield skink' and, scientifically, by several authors under the name Oligosoma aff. infrapunctatum "Chesterfield". Melzer et al. (2019) formally described this species, and coined the name Oligosoma salmo for this taxon.

Two sub-species are sometimes recognised: Capoetobrama k. orientalis was found in Kazakhstan, in the Chu River from the lower reaches to the region of Frunze. Capoetobrama k. kuschakewitschi was found in the Syr Darya (up to Kara Darya at Balykchi) and Amu Darya (upto Panj), and Zeravshan rivers, in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan (Bogutskaya, pers. comm.), Afghanistan and Uzbekistan. Both are treated as conspecific here.
This species was previously included in the genus Hyla but has recently been moved to the new genus Isthmohyla (Faivovich et al. 2005).

Mannophryne olmonae is not closely related to Mannophryne trinitatis (Lehtinen et al. 2011, Jowers et al. 2011), as was previously thought (Murphy 1997). Chromosome banding pattern data clearly allow a distinction between M. olmonae and Trinidadian M. trinitatis (Kaiser et al. 2003). These two species are not sister taxa; the sister taxon of M. olmonae is Mannophryne riveroi from the Peninsula de Paria, Venezuela (Lehtinen et al. 2011, Jowers et al. 2011).

Ninox squamipila, N. hypogramma, N. hantu and N. forbesi (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as N. squamipila following Norman et al. (1998), and before then were also lumped with N. natalis as N. squamipila following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993). Formerly considered conspecific with N. squamipila (which see), but separable on morphological and plumage details, molecular differences and perhaps voice (Norman et al. 1998). Monotypic.
This is a split from the broader concept of Isthmura belli, of which it was previously considered a subspecies (Rovito et al. 2015).
The taxonomic validity of this species is not clear (G. Parra-Olea and D. Wake pers. comm.).

Based on allozymes and mtDNA, this is one of the most distinct species of Mexican ambystomatids. It was previously thought to be a species complex, however, this was resolved by Weisrock et al. (2006) and this is not the case.

Genus placement under Exyrias is uncertain but possibly correct (Larson and Buckle 2012). This species is also considered species inquirenda in Exyrias by Kottelat (2013). Morphological examination is needed to ascertain the genus of this species.
This taxon was treated as a subpopulation of the European Grayling (Thymallus thymallus) prior to its description (Persat et al. 2019).
Described by Fischer (1804), this species was treated as a junior synonym of either Tarsius spectrum or T. tarsier until it was resurrected by Groves and Shekelle (2010).
A second species of Aenigmachanna, A. mahabali described by Kumar et al. (2019) is now a synonym of A. gollum (Raghavan et al. 2022).

authority: Bogutskaya, Jelić, Vucić, Jelić, Diripasko, Stefanov & Klobučar, 2019
taxonomicNotes:
The Channel Minnow (Phoxinus phoxinus), formerly Common or Eurasian Minnow, was for a considerable period of time treated as the only European member of the genus Phoxinus. However, at least 23 distinct mitochondrial lineages and 14 valid species have been identified in the region since the mid-2000s. This diversity is likely to increase further, as comprehensive information for all major European river systems has not yet been compiled. Moreover, additional sampling plus morphological analyses are required to corroborate some putative species divisions which are currently supported only by inconclusive nuclear data (Denys et al. 2020, Palandačić et al. 2017, 2020, 2022, Bogutskaya et al. 2023).

Taxonomic determination has been further hampered by natural phenotypic variability within the different lineages, plus their disparate geographic distributions which do not generally reflect patterns observed in related European fish genera. Furthermore, anthropogenic translocations linked to recreational fisheries have in some cases led to uncertainty regarding native range boundaries and driven introgressive hybridisation between congeners (Museth et al. 2007, Knebelsberger et al. 2015, Miró and Ventura 2015, Ramler et al. 2017, Vucić et al. 2018, Corral-Lou et al. 2019, Palandačić et al. 2020, 2022, De Santis et al. 2021).

As a result of the increasing species diversity, much of the published literature referring to Phoxinus phoxinus in fact pertains to other taxa and should therefore be reviewed with due care.
Taxonomic research is ongoing to determine whether all subpopulations are conspecific (Rajkumar K.P. pers comm. October 2020).
Many museum specimens assigned to Bufo beddomii are misidentifications (Biju 2001).

This is a restricted concept of this species following the reallocation of syntypes, previously assigned to this species, to Indirana sarojamma (Dahanukar et al. 2016). Records from Maharashtra have been re-assigned to Indirana chiravasi (Dahanukar et al. 2016).
This taxon has been moved to the genus Walkerana (Dahanukar et al. 2016).
This taxon has been moved to the genus Walkerana (Dahanukar et al. 2016).

The holotype of this species is lost, and the designation of a neotype is necessary if this proves to be a valid species. Rao (1937) originally described this species as Philautus elegans, but Bossuyt and Dubois (2001) transferred it from the genus Philautus to Micrixalus.
Some records attributed to this species might not belong to it (India Red List Assessment Workshop 2004).

The original description of this species, as Nyctibatrachus hussaini (Krishnamurthy et al. 2001), did not provide any information about the type specimen. Hence, its taxonomy and nomenclature required further investigation and amendments (Biju 2001, Das and Kunte 2005, S.K. Dutta pers. comm.). Dinesh et al. (2007) provided the replacement name Nyctibatrachus karnatakaensis.
This species was designated a lectotype and its range redelimited by Biju et al. (2011).
Biju et al. (2011) has revised the taxonomy of this species and designated a lectotype.
The holotype of this species is lost, hence Biju et al. (2011) designated a specimen collected in 2007 at Kempholey, Hassan district, Karnataka State as a neotype.

Research into the species validity needs to be prioritised. The key recommended conservation measures include taxonomic research on the generic allocation of this taxon (Das 1998, Chandramouli 2017, Harikrishnan and Vasudevan 2018).

Bossuyt and Dubois (2001) suggested that this species could be a synonym of Ixalus beddomii Günther, 1876. However, subsequent studies indicate that both species are distinct (Biju and Bossuyt 2009, Garg et al. 2021).
Bossuyt and Dubois (2001) designated a neotype for this species after the type specimen was lost.

Raorchestes punctatus and R. melanensis (collected by Rao in Karnataka) are considered to be synonyms of this species (Bossuyt and Dubois 2001), but further studies are required to confirm this relationship (S.D. Biju pers. comm.).

taxonomicNotes:
The species named Fejervarya nicobariensis in the 2004 and 2006 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species was in fact Hylarana nicobariensis. The true Fejervarya nicobariensis was inadvertently omitted from the 2004 and 2006 IUCN Red Lists. In 2008 it was assessed. The validity of the species was affirmed by Dubois and Ohler (2000).

This taxon has been moved to the genus Minervarya (Sanchez et al. 2018). There is still some taxonomic uncertainty regards this species, and in particular the range limits need to be determined (S.R. Chandramouli pers. comm. 2020).
This species has been resurrected from the synonymy of Nyctibatrachus beddomii by Biju et al. (2007).
This species was recently removed from the synonymy of Kaloula baleata (Chandramouli and Prasad 2018).

Rao (1937) originally described this taxon as Philautus kottigeharensis based on a single specimen from Kottigehar. Bossuyt and Dubois (2001) transferred the species from Philautus to Micrixalus. The holotype was lost and recently Bossuyt and Milinkovitch (2001) relocated the species from Bhadrea in Chicamangalore District very near to the type locality. 

Micrixalus narainensis and M. swamianus have been synonymised with this species by Biju et al. (2014).
This is a restricted concept of this species following the revalidation of Nyctibatrachus anamallaiensis which was previously placed in synonymy with this species (Biju et al. 2007).
Generic synonym = Capromys.
There is a question as to whether both Pseudoeurycea orchileucos and Pseudoeurycea orchimelas are distinct, valid species.

Low levels of genetic divergence between Indian Ocean Cryptoblepharus (Rocha et al. 2006) and difficulties in morphologically differentiating several forms (including the Comoran C. b. ater and C. b. mohelicus – F. Glaw pers. comm. June 2011) suggest the validity of many forms identified by Horner (2007) - who revised the genus and identified 54 species within it - requires further investigation, and the species recognized by Horner (2007) are not widely accepted by workers in the Indian Ocean region (e.g. Blom et al. 2019, Augros and Hawlitschek 2019).

The assessments for this group nonetheless follow the taxonomy proposed by Horner (2007) pending a more detailed revision of Indian Ocean Crypotoblepharus. Prior to the Horner revision, specific status was previously proposed for the Madagascan C. cognatus and C. voeltzkowi and supported by significant morphological differences (Andreone and Greer 2002), but this has not been widely adopted within the region and the taxonomy of these forms remains among the most controversial in the genus.

Recent genetic evidence from a biogeographic paper (Blom et al. 2019) confirms that genetic divergence within Indian Ocean Cryptoblepharus is low, but does not sample all nominal taxa and their results suggest that divergence - including that between C. cognatus and C. voeltzkowi - is comparable to that among Pacific Cryptoblepharus lineages recognized as full species (G. Shea pers. comm. 2020).
It is likely that this form consists of two separate species (G. Parra-Olea and D. Wake pers. comm.).
This species was previously included in the genus Hyla but has been moved to the new genus Charadrahyla (Faivovich et al. 2005).
This is a split from the broader concept of Sarcohyla thorectes (Grünwald et al. 2019).

A single subadult specimen (FMNH 64646) from the northeastern slopes of the Cordillera de Montecillos, Depto. Comayagua, was tentatively assigned to Bolitoglossa celaque sensu lato by McCranie and Wilson (2002), and, based on the presumed provenance of the specimen (ca 25 km NNE of the nearest locality for B. copinhorum), this specimen is tentatively referred to as B. copinhorum (Itgen et al. 2019).
Craterocephalus laisapi resembles but is distinct and different from C. centralis and C. cuneiceps from central and western Australia (Larson et al. 2005).

Nantis indefessus was transferred to Bryconamericus by Thomaz et al. (2015) based on a molecular phylogeny with weak support for that nomenclature change. Furthermore, Mirande (pers. comm.) stated "Thomaz et al. used DNA data from specimens of the lot LBP7123, identified at that moment as Bryconamericus exodon, the type species of the genus. However, those specimens were subsequently identified as B. iheringii. Therefore, all nomenclatural changes made by Thomaz et al. involving Bryconamericus are wrong. In particular, the synonymy of Hypobrycon, Nantis, and Odontostoechus with Bryconamericus are an artifact of that misidentification and those genera were, indeed resurrected by Mirande (2019)."

Thus, Mirande (2019), based on a more comprehensive phylogenetic analysis, resurrected Nantis showing that Bryconamericus exodon, the type species of the genus was placed in a different phylogenetic position from Thomaz et al. (2015) far from the clade including Nantis, and therefore showing that the inclusion of Nantis indefessus in Bryconamericus was wrong and unjustified. Therefore, the valid name of this species is Nantis indefessus.

Silfvergrip (2009) described the diagnostic features of A. japonica greater than 200 mm total length (TL). The mouth is small, about one fourth of head length, and distance from anus to end of tail is 5.6–6.0 times longer than distance from anus to dorsal fin insertion.

Even though some previous studies have treated Limia as one of the multiple subgenera in the genus Poecilia (Rosen and Bailey 1963, Meredith et al. 2010, Meredith et al. 2011), several other works have supported the generic classification for Limia (Rodriguez 1997, Hamilton 2001, Poeser 2003, Palacios et al. 2016, Weaver et al. 2016). Here we endorse the latter assessment that Limia should be considered a valid, separate genus.

The taxonomic role of genera to express relationships among species is clearly justified in the case of Limia from different points of view. From the biogeographic point of view, species of Limia show a discrete distribution since they are only found in the Antilles, specifically on Hispaniola, Cuba, Jamaica and the island of Grand Cayman. However, only three species of Poecilia sensu strictu occur in this region and they are restricted exclusively to Hispaniola. In addition, recent phylogenetic analyses have found Limia to be a monophyletic group probably originated from a South American ancestor with the three Hispaniolan Poecilia species mentioned above representing the closest sister group (Palacios et al. 2016, Weaver et al. 2016). A very detailed analysis is currently in prep, also confirming Limia as monophyletic (Spikes et al. in prep). Moreover, there is enough morphological distinctiveness in characters with adaptive value such is the case of gonopodial traits to separate species of Limia and Poecilia (Rivas 1978). Furthermore, all of the existing ecological and behavioral literature is using Limia, not Poecilia. Not recognizing Limia as a separate genus from Poecilia may obscure their similarities and cause even more confusion in a group that in fact deserves more taxonomic attention.

This species was originally differentiated as a new form by Dr John A. Endler. In 1975 during his field activities in Venezuela and the Island of Trinidad, in order to study different aspects of natural selection in Poecilia reticulata (see Endler 1978, 1980, 1983 among others), Endler made collections of this new form in the Laguna de Los Patos, adjacent to the city of Cumaná, Sucre State, Venezuela. These preserved and living specimens were brought to the United States and delivered to Dr Donn E. Rosen (AMNH) for study and description, as well as to Dr. Klaus Kallman for reproduction. The species was not described by Dr. Rosen, due to his death, but Dr. Kallman took it upon himself to distribute them to numerous ornamental fish breeders in different parts of the world, and the undescribed species began to be marketed and known as Endler's Livebearer or Endler's Guppy since the 1970s (Endler 2011).

The species was described as Poecilia wingei by Poeser, Kempkes & Isbrücker (2005), with specimens captured in 2002, in the hydrographic system of the Campoma and Buena Vista lagoons, (Sucre state, Venezuela), as well as other small coastal rivers close by.

Poecilia wingei is currently a valid species, considered a sister species to P. reticulata (Morris et al. 2018). Since its description, this species has not undergone nomenclatural modifications or generic relocations.

However, it is important to know that Herdeguen et al. (2014) do not consider Poecilia wingei as a valid or separate species of Poecilia reticulata, since they did not find sufficient genetic evidence that can separate or differentiate these two species. Other authors (Alexander and Breden 2004, Alexander et al. 2006, Ward et al. 2008, Tripathi et al. 2009a, b, Watson et al. 2010) do not consider P. wingei as a valid species, although they accept Poecilia reticulata populations from the north-eastern region of Venezuela, present in the aquatic ecosystems adjacent and close to the city of Cumaná and those of the Río Campoma basin (called by them Cumaná Guppy), as a case of incipient speciation (Alexander and Breden 2004, Herdeguen et al. 2014). According to Huber (2019), P. wingei is a typical “molecular species”, not diagnosable by some pattern or combination of external characters.

The genus Janetaescincus was established by Greer (1970), and is endemic to the Seychelles. The two nominal species in this genus are frequently treated as a single species, J. braueri, following Cheke (1984) and a series of subsequent resurrections and re-synonymizations (Bowler et al. 2006). The first genetic study on this genus suggests greater divergence than is represented by a two-species model, with at least three lineages on Silhouette alone (Harris et al. 2015). These authors recommend recognizing considering Janetaescincus as a single species complex under the name J. braueri, pending further taxonomic research.

For the sake of taxonomic stability, these assessments retain the two-species approach adopted in prior Red List assessments pending clarification of species boundaries, with the caveat that neither a one- nor a two-species model accurately reflects our current understanding of diversity in this group (S. Rocha and J. Harris pers. comms. 2020).

taxonomicNotes:
McGuire et al. (2019) review in detail the status of the all-white taxon occidentalis, which although formerly given species status (‘Great White Heron’ [GWH]) has long been considered a subspecies of Great Blue Heron [GBH] Ardea herodias, in great part because the two taxa interbreed with regularity. However, given that the evidence points to assortative mating where possible, they conclude that occidentalis is indeed better treated as a species:

it is separated by diagnostic plumage (white vs. blue), behaviour (mate choice and timing of mating) and habitat (saltwater-island vs. fresh/brackish water mainland).

There are, in fact, a few additional morphological considerations, with GWH having a shorter occipital plume but longer bill, tarsus and middle toe than GBH (supplementary material online with measurements not accessed). Applying the Tobias criteria to the situation, the taxonomic status of GWH involves a consideration of its

·       all-white vs grey/blue plumage (an exceptional difference: score 4);
·       shorter occipital plume (seemingly fairly distinctive from the authors’ Figure 3: allow 1);
·       longer tarsus (apparently the most distinctive of the longer characters measured, but perhaps insufficient to be allowed a score: ns);
·       timing of mating or habitat choice (only one of these permitted as a score: 1);
·       narrow hybrid zone (not more than 50 km as measured on Google Earth: 2).

On this basis BirdLife accepts Ardea occidentalis (Handbook of the Birds of the World and BirdLife International 2020) as a separate species.

So far, there have been six genetic studies undertaken on rockhopper penguins using different genetic technics and analysis (Banks et al. 2006; Jouventin et al. 2006; de Dinechin et al. 2009, Frugone et al. 2018, Mays et al. 2019, Lois et al. 2020). Jouventin et al. (2006) found only significant genetic differentiation between the northern and southern/ eastern populations. However, Banks et al. (2006) identified three species, and proposed a further split of E. chrysocome into southern (E. chrysocome) and eastern (E. filholi) ‘species’. This was not adopted by BirdLife International on the grounds of small sample sizes and limited morphological differences between the southern and eastern forms (BirdLife International 2008). However, further research by de Dinechin et al. (2009) also supported the split of chrysocome and filholi.
Recently, Frugone et al. (2018) analyzed two mtDNA (HVRI, COI) and two nuclear (ODC, AK1) markers from 13 locations of five putative Eudyptes species: rockhopper (E. filholi, E. chrysocome, and E. moseleyi), macaroni (E. chrysolophus) and royal penguins (E. schlegeli). They found a strong phylogeographic structure among rockhopper penguins from South America, subantarctic and subtropical islands supporting the recognition of three separate species of rockhopper penguins. Mays et al. (2019), on the other hand, using similar markers but different modelling also found genetic structure and low genetic flow, but in his analyses the best-supported population models for the southern rockhoppers combined E. c. chrysocome and E. c. filholi into a single lineage or 2 lineages with bidirectional gene flow, and thus proposed that they should be treated as different management units only. Lois et al. (2020) added new information on the southern rockhopper (E. c. chrysocome) from the southwest Atlantic Ocean. Studying the genetic structure of individuals from different colonies located in the southwest Atlantic they found evidence for two genetic clusters within the rockhopper, one northern (Falkland/ Malvinas Islands and Isla Pingüino) and one southern (Terhalten and Staten Island).

Monotypic.

Recent phylogenetic analyses have shown that the species shows little genetic divergence from Royal Penguin populations (Frugone et al. 2018; 2019), suggesting that a reappraisal of the taxonomic status is needed.

This species was revalidated in 2014, after a series of studies highlighted genetic and morphological disparities between grayling subpopulations from the northern Adriatic region and elsewhere in Europe (Sušnik et al. 2001, 2004, Geiger et al. 2014, Bianco 2014).

Earlier publications referring to graylings from the northern Adriatic as T. thymallus thus correspond to T. aeliani and/or hybrid individuals (see 'Population').
This is a split from the broader concept of Andrias davidianus (Turvey et al. 2019).
This species is in the Dryophytes immaculatus group, and is a split from the broader concept of Dryophytes suweonensis (Borzée et al. 2020).

This is a restricted concept of Gastrotheca litonedis following the split of the broader concept into this and G. cuencana based on the discrete morphological and acoustic differences between the two species (Carvajal-Endara et al. 2019).
This is the new broader concept including Centrolene scirtetes and C. gemmatum synonymised with this species, following Guayasamin et al. (2020).
Rediscovered in 2002, after more than 120 years with virtually no sightings or data of any sort (Mauro 2005). Monotypic.
The genus Ebenavia was revised by Hawlitschek et al. (2018). These authors described a lineage endemic to the Comoros previously included within E. inunguis as the new species E. tuelinae.

Paroedura sanctijohannis was previously considered to occur on all four islands in the Comoros Archipelago, and this scheme was adopted in a previous Red List assessment (Hawlitschek and Glaw 2011) The population from Mayotte has since been described as the new species P. stellata (Hawlitschek and Glaw 2012).

Paroedura sanctijohannis was previously considered to occur on all four islands in the Comoros Archipelago, and this scheme was adopted in a previous Red List assessment (Hawlitschek and Glaw 2011) The population from Mayotte has since been described as the new species P. stellata (Hawlitschek and Glaw 2012).
Lötters (1996), suggested that the Cauca localities (by Cochran and Goin 1970) were doubtful on geographic grounds.
Calyptophilus frugivorus and C. tertius (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as C. frugivorus following Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).

Previously listed as Poeoptera femoralis (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) and before that as Cinnyricinclus femoralis. Also previously placed in genus Pholia. Treating Pholia and Arizelospar in Poeoptera following Lovette and Rubenstein (2007) would render Poeoptera a large entity with unusually deep branch lengths. We follow WGAC in resurrecting the monotypic genus Arizelospar Oberholser 1905 for this distinctive species. Monotypic.
Treron australis and T griveaudi (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as T. australis following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993).

In the past, the eastern Brazilian marmosets (penicillata É. Geoffroy, 1812; geoffroyi É. Geoffroy in Humboldt, 1812; aurita É. Geoffroy in Humboldt, 1812; and flaviceps Thomas, 1903) of the ‘jacchus group’ were considered to be subspecies of Callithrix jacchus, following Hershkovitz (1977). All taxa were later elevated to full species level (Coimbra-Filho 1984, Mittermeier et al. 1988, Marroig et al. 2004, Coimbra-Filho et al. 2006).

Coimbra-Filho (1986a, b, 1990, 1991) has argued that the similarity in dental morphology (Natori 1986), behaviour, pelage (infants of the two forms are practically identical in appearance), vocalizations (Mendes 1997b,c) and the recent discovery of wild groups of hybrids between C. aurita and C. flaviceps at Carangola, Minas Gerais (Ferrari and Mendes 1991), suggest subspecific status (Coimbra-Filho et al. 1993). Ferrari et al. (1996) studied and reviewed the ecology and behaviour of C. aurita and C. flaviceps groups and concluded that although undoubtedly very similar, the “comparison appears to have done more to re-emphasize the enormous flexibility underlying the behavioural ecology of the marmosets as a whole than clarify the relationships between these two taxa in particular”. Here, Rylands’ (2012) proposed taxonomy is followed; it considers C. aurita and C. flaviceps as full species.

The validity and authorship of the name Callithrix kuhlii has been the subject of some debate. Hershkovitz (1975, p.142) was the first to indicate that Wied-Neuwied (1826) had referred to the marmoset of south-east Bahia as “Hapale penicillata Kuhlii” [sic]. However, Hershkovitz (1975, 1977) argued at length that kuhlii was not a valid taxon, being merely an intergrade between C. j. penicillata and C. j. geoffroyi. Vivo (1991, pp.80-81), on the other hand, argued that Wied-Neuwied (1826) had not intentionally given it this name, merely, and incorrectly, ascribing the authorship of the name penicillatato Kuhl. The first person to intentionally use the name kuhlii to describe the marmosets from south-east Bahia was Hershkovitz (1975), but his argument that it was not a valid taxonomic entity disqualifies the possibility of him being attributed authorship. This is therefore given to Coimbra-Filho (1985). A full description of the species is given in Coimbra-Filho et al. (2006).

In the past, the eastern Brazilian marmosets (penicillata É. Geoffroy, 1812, geoffroyi É. Geoffroy in Humboldt, 1812, aurita É. Geoffroy in Humboldt, 1812, and flaviceps Thomas, 1903) of the “jacchus group” were considered to be subspecies of Callithrix jacchus, following Hershkovitz (1977). All are now considered to be full species (see Coimbra-Filho 1984, Mittermeier et al. 1988, Marroig et al. 2004, Coimbra-Filho et al. 2006).
Geobiastes squamiger (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Brachypteracias. Gender agreement of species name follows David and Gosselin (2002b).

Laterallus rogersi (Handbook of the Birds of the World and BirdLife International 2020) was previously in the genus Atlantisia (del Hoyo and Collar 2014). Stervander et al. (2019) found that this species, Dot-winged Crake Porzana spiloptera and Yellow-breasted Crake Hapalocrex flaviventer nest within a clade of Laterallus crakes, with the first two grouped closely with Black Rail Laterallus jamaicensis. It thus appears appropriate to move all three species to the genus Laterallus, and this option is adopted here. Monotypic.
Zapornia olivieri (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Amaurornis.

Gallinula nesiotis and G. comeri (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as G. nesiotis following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993) and Groenenburg et al. (2008, 2009), and before that had been treated as separate species by Collar and Stuart (1985).

authority: Townsend, Herrera-B., Hofmann, Luque-Montes, Ross, Dudek, Krygeris, Duchamp & Wilson, 2020
taxonomicNotes: This is a split from the broader concept of Atlantihyla spinipollex (Townsend et al. 2020).

The use of this name has been clarified by McCranie and Wilson (1993). This species was moved from Ptychohyla to Atlantihyla (Faivovich et al. 2018). This is a restricted concept of Atlantihyla spinipollex following the split of the broader concept into this and A. melissa (Townsend et al. 2020).
This species was elevated to species status by La Marca (1983).

The nomenclatural history of this species was detailed by Lötters et al. (1998) and Lötters and La Marca (2001). This species was redescribed by Lötters, La Marca and Vences (2004) after the discovery that the original type material represented Atelopus varius of Central America. The former junior synonym Atelopus vogli is considered to be a distinct species following (Lötters et al. 2004)

Until now, this species had not been included in any phylogenetic study, and its relationships with Rhinella alata and the others members of Rhinella margaritifera group are still unknown (dos Santos et al. 2015). The records of “Bufo typhonius alatus” from Curimagua (Falcón state) and Bejuma (Carabobo state) by Rivero (1961, 1964) may correspond to Rhinella sclerocephala.
In the Centrolene prosoblepon group according to Ruíz-Carranza and Lynch (1991), and Cisneros-Heredia and McDiarmid (2006).
Based on a molecular phylogeny, Guayasamin et al. (2009) reallocated this species in the genus Vitreorana.

Based on a molecular phylogeny, Guayasamin et al. (2009) described the new genus Celsiella to reallocate two endemic species – C. revocata and C. vozmedianoi - from the northern mountain system in Venezuela.

Based on its phylogenetic position, and characterized by its combination of the molecular synapomorphies and some morphological characteristics, this species was assigned to Vitreorana, and designated as the type species of this genus (Guayasamin et al. 2009).
This species had been included in phylogenetic studies by Guayasamin et al. (2008, 2009), and Castroviejo-Fisher et al. (2014).

In the genus Hyalinobatrachium based on morphological and behavioral characteristics (Señaris and Ayarzagüena 2005, Guayasamin et al. 2009). Until now this species has not been included in any phylogenetic study.

Originally described in the genus Centrolenella (Rivero, 1985). Ruiz-Carranza and Lynch (1991) transferred this species to Hyalinobatrachium, and posteriorly to the genus Cochranella (Ruíz-Carranza and Lynch 1998). Based on a molecular phylogeny of the family Centrolenidae, Guayasamin et al. (2009) described the genus Celsiella to reallocate this species (as the type species of the genus) and other endemic glass frog from the northern mountain system in Venezuela: C. vozmedianoi.

Originally assigned to Phyllobates (Test 1956) but subsequently transferred to Colostethus by Edwards (1971), and to Allobates by Grant et al. (2006). In both cases, taxonomic changes were based only on morphological evidence. Its phylogenetic position and its relationships with other Allobates species are unknown as this species has not yet been included in any quantitative phylogenetic study.

Originally described as a member of Phyllobates (Schmidt 1932) but subsequently transferred to Prostherapis (Rivero 1961), Colostethus (Edwards 1971), and finally to Allobates (Grant et al. 2006) where is currently allocated (Frost 2020). Although the last change was made in the contexts of an exhaustive phylogenetic study (Grant et al. 2006) this species was not included in the analyses and its reallocation was only based on its overall morphological similarity with other Allobates. Therefore, its phylogenetic relationships remain unknown and its generic position should be considered provisional and pending corroboration.

Originally described as Hyloxalus collaris by Boulenger (1912) (misspelled Hylixalus). Successively moved to Prostherapis and Colostetus by Rivero (1961) and Edwards (1971), respectively, and finally allocated in Mannophryne by La Marca (1992), where still remains. Its taxonomic position has been corroborated in two recent phylogenetic studies (Grant et al. 2017, Rojas-Runjaic 2019).
Since its description (La Marca 1994) it has not undergone taxonomic changes. Its taxonomic position has been corroborated in two recent phylogenetic studies (Santos et al. 2014, Grant et al. 2017).

Originally described as Prostherapis neblina by Test (1956) and subsequently transferred to Colostethus by Edwards (1971) and to Mannophryne by La Marca (1992). Its phylogenetic position, as part of Mannophryne, has been recently corroborated by Rojas-Runjaic (2019).

Previous to Grant et al. (2006) the genus Aromobates was known only by a single species: A. nocturnus (Myers et al. 1991). Then, Grant et al. (2006) moved all Colostethus of the alboguttatus group (sensu Rivero 1988) or Nephelobates (sensu La Marca 1994) to Aromobates and provided a well-corroborated phylogeny of the genus. Barrio-Amorós and Santos (2012) provide a phylogeny and a list with current threats for all species of the genus. Rivero (1982a) included Colostehus inflexus Rivero, 1978 in the synonymy of C. alboguttatus. Myers, Paolillo and Daly (1991) and La Marca (1997) revive the species as Nephelobates inflexus in their works without explanation. Recently, Barrio-Amorós and Santos (2012) consider inflexus different from A. alboguttatus and a valid species, but without supporting evidence.

Originally described under the genus Colostethus by Rivero (1980). It was transferred to Nephelobates by La Marca (1994) and most recently reallocated to Aromobates by Grant et al. (2006). Its phylogenetic position (as part of Aromobates) has been corroborated by Rojas-Runjaic (2019).

Originally described under the genus Colostethus by Dole and Durant (1972). It was transferred to Nephelobates by La Marca (1994) and lastly reallocated to Aromobates by Grant et al. (2006). Its phylogenetic position (as part of Aromobates) has been corroborated by Barrio-Amorós and Santos (2012), Grant et al. (2017), and Rojas-Runjaic (2019).
It can be distinguished from other species of the genus by the skin co-ossified with the skull and transverse occipital ridge bearing spinous elevations (Duellman 1980).

It can be distinguished from other species of the genus by triangular dermal calcar present on heel and triangular dermal process present on margin of eyelid (Duellman 1980). It could be a junior synonym of Gastrotheca williamsoni, so its taxonomic status requires further investigation (Barrio-Amorós et al. 2019).

Originally described as a member of Hyla by Rivero (1961) and then transferred to the resurrected genus Hyloscirtus by Faivovich et al. (2005) on the basis of morphological evidence. Its phylogenetic position was corroborated by Rojas-Runjaic et al. (2018) using molecular data. Centrolenella estevesi Rivero, 1968 is a junior synonym of this species (Barrio-Amorós et al. 2019).

Originally described as a subspecies of Hyla vilsoniana by Rivero (1961) and later elevated to the species level by Duellman (1989), who also assigned it to the labialis group. It was moved to the genus Dendropsophus by Faivovich et al. (2005) on the basis of molecular phylogenetic evidence. According to Guarnizo et al. (2012), D. pelidnus could be a junior synonym of this species but it is still considered valid for this assessment.

This species was transferred to Agalychnis by Faivovich et al. (2010), but was not assigned to any species group. Until now this leaf frog is still missing in phylogenetic analyses and its evolutionary relationships are unknown.

In the Pristimantis (Pristimantis) unistrigatus species group by Hedges et al. (2008). This species has not been included in any phylogenetic study, and has not been assigned to any species group in the last molecular analysis of the New World direct-developing frogs of Padial et al. (2014). In the family Strabomantidae sensu Heinicke et al. (2018).

Originally described in the genus Hylodes by Peters (1863), and subsequently transferred to Eleutherodactylus by Stejneger (1904) and Pristimantis by Heinicke et al. (2007) where it is currently placed (Frost 2020). Not assigned to any species group by Hedges et al. (2008) or Padial et al. (2014). Its evolutionary relationships within Pristimantis are unknown as it has not been included in any phylogenetic analysis. According to Lynch and La Marca (1993), Eleutherodactylus lancini Rivero 1961, E. racenisi Rivero 1961, and E. williamsi Rivero 1961, are junior synonyms of this species. Lynch and La Marca (1993) further suggested that Eleutherodactylus rozei Rivero 1961 could be an additional junior synonym of Pristimantis reticulatus, but this must be evaluated.

La Marca (2007) erected the genus Paramophrynella for this and related species. This genus had been considered a synonym of Pristimantis by Hedges et al. (2008), and later Barrio-Amorós et al. (2013) reinforced this synonym with molecular data. Not assigned to any species group by Padial et al. (2014).

The species was named in 1965 by Roberto Donoso Barros as Eleutherodactylus lancinii, but the formal description was published later (Donoso-Barros, 1968). Other descriptions are in Rivero (1982) and La Marca (2007). La Marca (2007) created the new genus Mucubatrachus for this and related species, that was afterwards regarded as a synonym of Pristimantis by Hedges et al. (2008) and later confirmed by molecular data (Barrio-Amorós et al. 2013).

La Marca (2007) recently erected the genus Mucubatrachus to accommodate species that have a dermal fold posterior to the urostyle and before the cloaca. Hedges et al. (2008), however, subsequently placed Mucubatrachus in the synonymy of Pristimantis.

Originally described as a member of Eleutherodactylus (Walker and Test 1955) and later transferred to Pristimantis (Heinicke et al. 2007). Hedges et al. (2008) and Padial et al. (2014) also listed this species as part of Pristimantis but did not assign it to any species group as it was not included in their phylogenetic analyses. Its evolutionary relationships remain unknown.

There are two available descriptions for this frog: Eleutherodactylus vanadise by La Marca (1984) and that of its synonym Eleutherodactylus cerasoventris (Rivero 1984 “1982”). Even though these descriptions were based on 29 and 36 specimens respectively, the variation in nature was not fully represented. Barrio-Amorós et al. (2013) reported four chromotypes, based on 98 specimens. In the Pristimantis unistrigatus species group according to the original publication (La Marca 1984) and Hedges et al. (2008); not assigned to any species group by Padial et al. (2014). In the Family Strabomantidae by Heinicke et al. (2018).

This species was the first endemic salamander described from Venezuela. It was described by Trapido in 1942 using a single specimen collected in the vicinity of the Borburata River Valley in Carabobo state. This author suggested that a specimen from Río San Esteban, Carabobo state, was B. borburata and not B. altamazonica as previously suggested by Dunn (1926). Specimens reported from Falcón state (Linares 1974, Mijares-Urrutia and Arends 2000) and Yaracuy state (Barrio-Amorós 1999, Lotzkat 2007) might represent a different taxon (Mijares-Urrutia and Arends 2000, Barrio-Amorós et al. 2019). We tentatively consider the populations from Yaracuy as part of the same taxon although a taxonomic assessment is required. The phylogenetic position of this species is unclear. Parra-Olea et al. (2004) assigned this species to the B. (Eladinea) adspersa group based on its South American distribution.

Schargel et al. (2002) mentioned that this species is morphologically more similar to B. adspersa, B. borburata, B. savagei, B. taylori, and B. vallecula than the geographically close species, B. orestes. Apparently, such difference is also applicable to the most recently described species B. mucuyensis, which is the sister species of B. orestes (García-Gutiérrez et al. 2013). This species was tentatively assigned to the B. adspersa group by Schargel et al. (2002). Parra-Olea et al. (2004) placed B. guaramacalensis in the B. (Eladinea) adspersa group based on its South American distribution.

In the Pristimantis unistrigatus species group of Hedges et al. (2008), but not assigned to any species group by Padial et al. (2014). In the Pristimantis conspicillatus group (Barrio-Amorós et al. 2019). In the Family Strabomantidae by Heinicke et al. (2018).

This species was originally described as Colostethus caribe, but a year later was moved to the genus Allobates based on its morphological characteristics (Lötters et al. 2007).

Lötters et al. (2007: 60) in an apparent transcription mistake made reference to this species as Anomaloglossus caribe.

La Marca (2007) erected the genus Mucubatrachus to accommodate species that have a dermal fold posterior to the urostyle and before the cloaca. Hedges et al. (2008), however, subsequently placed Mucubatrachus in the synonymy of Pristimantis. Pristimantis rhigophilus can be distinguished from other similar species by a combination of morphological characters and colour patterns (La Marca 2007).
It has not undergone taxonomic changes. Its phylogenetic position within Mannophryne has been corroborated by Rojas-Runjaic (2019).

Fermin et al. (2012) synonymized Bolitoglossa spongai (described by Barrio-Amorós and Fuentes-Ramos in 1999), also from Sierra La Culata, under B. orestes based on molecular evidence (16S, cytb and cox genes sequence analysis) and morphological data. Specimens from Sierra Nevada de Mérida, previously considered as B. orestes, are actually specimens of its sister species, B. mucuyensis (García-Gutiérrez et al. 2013). Bolitoglossa orestes was placed in the B. (Eladinea) adspersa group by Parra-Olea et al. (2004).

Since its description (Barrio-Amorós and Santos 2012) it has not undergone taxonomic changes. Its taxonomic position has been corroborated in two recent phylogenetic studies (Grant et al. 2017, Rojas-Runjaic 2019).

authority: García-Gutiérrez, Escalona, Mora, de Pascual & Fermin, 2013
taxonomicNotes: Specimens of this species were previously identified as B. orestes (Barrio-Amorós and Fuentes-Ramos 1999, García-Gutiérrez et al. 2013). The molecular and morphological analyses of Fermin et al. (2012) shed light on the species diversity and its known distribution in the vicinity of Mérida city. Thus, B. mucuyensis was described from La Mucuy region, at Sierra Nevada de Mérida, and B. orestes was restricted to the Sierra La Culata, the close parallel mountain chain (García-Gutiérrez et al. 2013). It is unclear if specimens from the road Mérida-El Morro, at Sierra Nevada de Mérida (stored at the Museo de Historia Natural La Salle, MHNLS), belong to B. mucuyensis. B. mucuyensis is the sister species of B. orestes and it is member of the B. adspersa group (García-Gutiérrez et al. 2013).
In the Pristimantis unistrigatus group according to the original description (Kaiser et al. 2015).

authority: Patton, Apodaca, Corser, Wilson, Williams, Cameron & Wake, 2019
taxonomicNotes: This is a split from the broader concept of Aneides aeneus (Patton et al. 2019).

Some specimens from Brazilian Amazonia were previously confused with both Atelopus pulcher (e.g., Gascon 1989, Zimmerman and Simberloff 1996) and Atelopus spumarius, both of which differ in morphology and advertisement call, and now belong to a separate species, Atelopus manauensis (Jorge et al. 2020).
This species was previously confused with both Atelopus pulcher and Atelopus spumarius (both of which differ in morphology and advertisement call), according to Jorge et al. (2020).
Clanga clanga (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Aquila.
This is a split from the broader concept of Litoria littlejohni (Mahony et al. 2020).

This taxon was considered a subspecies of Nycticebus coucang but elevated by Groves and Maryanto (2008). This is further supported by morphological studies by Nekaris and Jaffe (2007) and Nekaris and Munds (2010) and genetic studies by Roos (2003) and Wirdateti et al. (2006). Two distinct forms regularly occur in bird markets and further research is needed (Nekaris and Jaffe 2007). Care should be taken in taxonomic studies however due to translocation of individuals from markets into forests and gardens throughout the island (Schulze and Groves 2004). The distinct black and white long-haired appearance of subadults and juveniles also might be mistaken as separate species, for example, in museum specimens or from photos only (KA. Nekaris et al. pers. comm. 2012).
Was under Iguanidae.

Passer domesticus and P. italiae (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as P. domesticus following AERC TAC (2003); AOU (1998 & supplements); Christidis and Boles (2008); Cramp et al. (1977–1994); Dowsett and Forbes-Watson (1993); SACC (2005 & updates); Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993); Stotz et al. (1996); Turbott (1990).
This species was described by Hernández et al. (2000), but the name first appeared in Barbadillo et al. (1999) and this is therefore the correct authority.

authority: Lymberakis, Poulakakis, Kaliontzopoulou, Valakos and Mylonas, 2008

taxonomicNotes:
Although Schneider and Haxhiu (1994) had difficulty distinguishing the voice of Pelophylax shqipericus from that of P. lessonae, morphology, allozymes, mtDNA sequences, and crossing experiments all indicate that P. shqipericus is distinct from P. lessonae. The species belongs to “lessonae” group and it is sister species to P. lessonae - based on mtDNA and ND3 sequences, 1378 b.p. (Plötner et al. 2012).

This species does not make hybridogenetic hybrids (Guerrini et al. 1997).

Sometimes placed in genus Dryolimnas. Closely related to L. mirifica and L. pectoralis; on occasion regarded as subspecies of L. pectoralis, but differs in its much smaller wing (score estimated at 3); much reduced streaking on crown and hindneck (2); upperparts with sparser, narrower streaking (1); barring on upperwing-coverts reduced (1). Monotypic.
Hemignathus lucidus, H. hanapepe and H. affinis (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as H. lucidus following AOU (1998 & supplements); Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).
Has sometimes been thought to be closely related to S. serinus, S. canaria and S. canicollis, but recent DNA analyses recovered this species as sister to S. pusillus (Zuccon et al. 2012). Monotypic.
Coenocorypha aucklandica, C. huegeli, C. barrierensis and C. iredalei (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as C. aucklandica following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993).
Apparently closest to S. speluncae (Bornschein et al. 1998) (which see) and S. gonzagai. Monotypic.

Zanda baudinii (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Calyptorhynchus. Original note from Illustrated Checklists: Closely related to Z. funerea and Z. latirostris. Long considered conspecific with latter, but currently treated as separate species because ecology quite different, and bill significantly longer; difficulty in field identification, compounded by long history of conspecific treatment, has led to uncertainty regarding limits of range in area of overlap, and to publication of some inaccurate maps. Present species has also, on occasion, been lumped in Z. funerea. Confusion over bill size of specimen used in original description led to proposal of subspecies tenuirostris, but this name shown to be synonymous with baudinii (Schodde and Mason 1997). Monotypic.
Monotypic.
Unidentified Pipistrellus bats found in the Azores have recently been proposed to belong to this species, but this awaits confirmation.
Cyclopsitta diophthalma and C. coxeni (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as C. diophthalma following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993).

authority: Coloma, Duellman, Almendáriz, Ron, Terán-Valdez & Guayasamin, 2010

taxonomicNotes:
Gallirallus conditicius (Sibley and Monroe 1990, 1993), known only from the type reputedly collected in the Apiang Group of the Gilbert Islands, Kiribati, in 1861, is not recognised as a separate species but is treated as a synonym of H. sylvestris (Greenway 1952, Olson 1992).


Hypotaenidia sylvestris (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Gallirallus.
Psephotellus chrysopterygius (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Psephotus.

Zanda latirostris (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Calyptorhynchus. Original note from Illustrated Checklists: Closely related to Z. funerea and Z. baudinii. Long considered conspecific with latter, mainly on account of identical plumages (Juniper and Parr 1998), but currently treated as separate because present species’ ecology quite different and bill significantly shorter than that of Z. baudinii; difficulty in field identification, compounded by long history of conspecific treatment, has led to uncertainty regarding limits of range in area of overlap, and to publication of some inaccurate maps. Exhaustive analysis of all available specimens of taxa in present genus suggested that latirostris was so similar to South Australian Z. funerea that it might perhaps be treated as subspecies of latter. Monotypic.

Zapornia atra (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Porzana. In the past sometimes assigned to monotypic genus Nesophylax. Closely related to Z. tabuensis and Z. monasa. Monotypic.

Since 1930 commonly treated as a subspecies of C. auriceps, and clearly the two are closely related; present species differs, however, in its considerably larger size, with mean male wing 128.2 (n=6) vs 109.9 (n=10) (Forshaw 1989) (at least 2), its lack of red line between frons and eye (2), outer webs of flight-feathers greenish-blue vs violet-blue (2), and more yellowish underparts (1). Has hybridized extensively with C. novaezelandiae chathamensis, to the extent that it was almost eradicated by genetic swamping (Chan Chi-hang et al. 2005, Chan Chi-hang et al. 2006, Triggs and Daugherty 1996). Monotypic.

Hemiphaga novaeseelandiae and H. chathamensis (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as H. novaeseelandiae following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993). Usually considered conspecific with H. novaeseelandiae, but differs in its grey vs blue-green rump and primary wing-coverts (3); matt blackish-grey vs glossy dark green crown, throat, breast and neck-sides (3); reduced dull maroon carpal area (2); dark green vs whitish undertail-coverts (ns2); darker tail (ns1); much stouter bill (not measured, but estimated at 2); also modest genetic divergence (Goldberg et al. 2010). Monotypic.

Has frequently been considered a subspecies of H. unicolor or of H. ostralegus; differentiation relatively weak, and species status perhaps questionable. Recent study of mtDNA, however, supported treatment as a separate species (Banks and Paterson 2007). Form H. ostralegus finschi has on occasion been associated with present species. Monotypic.

Senior synonym A. maxima apparently unused for more than a century, now recommended for formal suppression (Palma et al. 2003). Monotypic.

Apteryx australis, A. mantelli and A. rowi (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously treated as A. australis and A. mantelli (incorporating rowi) following Baker et al. (1995); prior to that all three taxa were lumped as A. australis following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993). Nominate subspecies further divides into two genetically well-separated populations, based respectively on Haast R (plumage distinctively rufous) and Fiordland (plumage grey-brown) (Burbidge et al. 2003, Herbert and Daugherty 2002). Two subspecies currently recognized.

Six subspecies have been described (Ansell 1972; summarized in Cassinello 1998). However, apart from the fact that the morphological differences between them are not well defined, and there are several apparent zones of hybridization, relying exclusively on morphological traits is an obsolete and inadequate criterion to define subspecies. Therefore, and in order to re-evaluate aoudad subspecies distinction, a comprehensive genetic analysis of individuals from all the distinctive populations should be carried out. This would allow to properly identify genetic units that help redefining subspecific criteria and eventually allow undertaking proper conservation actions to protect the species (Cassinello 2015).

taxonomicNotes: López-Luna et al. (2018, 2021) described and characterized this range-restricted mud turtle (Kinosternon vogti) from the coastal Bahía de Banderas region of Jalisco, Mexico. Previously (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) placed in the genus Alopecoenas and before that in the genus Gallicolumba but transferred to Pampusana on the grounds of the latter’s priority (Bruce et al. 2016). Monotypic.
Otidiphaps nobilis, O. aruensis, O. cervicalis and O. insularis (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) were previously lumped as O. nobilis following Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993).

taxonomicNotes: Formerly included within C. ecaudatus, the specific status was recognised by Travouillon et al. (2019).

Edolisoma tenuirostre, E. insperatum, E. nesiotis, E. monacha, E. rostratum, E. meyerii, E. obiense, E. grayi, E. remotum and E. salomonis (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as Coracina tenuirostris following Christidis and Boles (2008) and Sibley and Monroe (1990, 1993).

The previous Red List assessments for Galápagos tortoises treated the various allopatric island populations as subspecies of Chelonoidis nigra, as did several authors (Pritchard 1996; Caccone et al. 1999; Beheregaray et al. 2003; Fritz and Havas 2007; TTWG 2007, Rhodin et al. 2008). However, other authors have considered them as full species based on morphology (Bour 1980; Fritts 1983; Ernst and Barbour 1989) and more recently several researchers (Caccone et al. 2002; Russello et al. 2005, 2007; Poulakakis et al. 2008, 2012, 2015; Chiari et al. 2009) have treated most of them as full species based on congruent patterns of mitochondrial and nuclear variation. This elevated species-level taxonomy has been largely accepted by TTWG (2009, 2014) and TEWG (2015) for most phylogenetic lineages of Galápagos tortoises. This Red List assessment therefore now treats C. abingdonii as a full species, rather than retaining its previous subspecies ranking from earlier Red List assessments.

Arnold et al. (2008) revised the taxonomy of this species, formerly considered the only endemic species of Hemidactylus on Cape Verde and including the subspecies Hemidactylus bouvieri boavistensis (Boavista and Sal) and H. b. razoensis (Santo Luzia and Raso) in addition to populations from Fogo and São Nicolau unassigned to any subspecies. These authors re-elevated H. b. boavistensis to full species status and described the Fogo population as a new species, H. lopezjuradoi. The São Nicolau population was retained within H. bouvieri on the basis that available material is too poorly-preserved to permit morphological description, but was found to be genetically distinct from typical H. bouvieri. Arnold et al. (2008) consider that once better material becomes available this form will warrant description as a distinct taxon.
Usually considered to be closest to D. pacifica, D. oceanica and D. aurorae. Monotypic.

taxonomicNotes:
This species was revalidated in 2021, having for several decades been considered to be a junior synonym of the Horse Barbel (Barbus tyberinus).

It shares an identical geographic range with the congeneric taxon Barbus oscensis Rossi and Plazzi 2021, which was described from the Ofanto River system and is considered valid by some published sources (e.g., Fricke et al. 2023). However, the studies which respectively revalidated B. fucini and described B. oscensis were published just a few weeks apart and are broadly comparable in terms of hypotheses, methodologies and outcomes (Lorenzoni et al. 2021, Rossi et al. 2021). For the purposes of this assessment, B. oscensis is therefore treated as a junior synonym of B. fucini, since the two taxa are understood to represent the same species and the latter is the earliest published name (also see Rondinini et al. 2022, from which B. oscensis is omitted).

Aerodramus bartschi (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was previously placed in the genus Collocalia. Collocalia inquieta (Sibley and Monroe 1990, 1993) was previously split into C. bartschi following Browning (1993) and AOU (1998) and C. inquieta following Browning (1993).
See A. vaughani. Monotypic.

This account follows the suggested Salamandra monophyletic group distribution presented in Steinfartz et al. (2000). See also Burgon et al. (2021).

The identity of some subpopulations of Salamandra species reported from western Anatolia (Türkiye) require further investigation and are not included within this concept, although Frost (2022) notes that it is expected to occur there.
Lalage leucomela and L. conjuncta (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as L. leucomela following Christidis & Boles (2008) and Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).
Manucerthia mana (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) was previously placed in the genus Oreomystis following AOU (1998 & supplements); Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).
Loxops coccineus, L. ochraceus and L. wolstenholmei (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) were previously lumped as L. coccineus following AOU (1998 & supplements); Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).
Nyctanassa carcinocatactes (del Hoyo and Collar 2014) was newly-described from fossil remains by Olson and Wingate (2006).
Hemignathus wilsoni (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) was previously listed as H. munroi following AOU (1998 & supplements); Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).

It has been argued, on the basis of mandibular measurements, that Crocidura canariensis should be treated as a subspecies of C. sicula (Sarà 1996). However, other morphological, ecological, palaeontological and molecular evidence supports specific status (Michaux et al. 1991, Hutterer et al. 1992). Genetic distances suggest that C. canariensis and C. sicula diverged approximately five million years ago (Vogel et al. 2003), and both share karyotype with C. tarfayaensis (Vogel et al. 2006).
Chlorodrepanis stejnegeri (del Hoyo and Collar 2016) was previously placed in the genus Hemignathus and listed as H. kauaiensis following AOU (1998 & supplements); Sibley & Monroe (1990, 1993).

Prior to its formal description, this taxon was referred to as Coregonus sp. "Albock", and has on occasion been misidentified as the congener C. fatioi.

Genetic evidence suggests that it may be partially allochthonous in origin, with ancestral contributions from congeneric species that are endemic to Lake Constance (de. Bodensee) but were occasionally stocked in Lake Thun until the mid-20th century.

At the regional scale, the systematics of European ciscoes and whitefishes (Coregonus spp.) has been the subject of considerable debate since the turn of the 21st century, with little indication of a definitive outcome.

It is widely accepted that non-anadromous members of this group have repeatedly undergone adaptive radiations in boreal, subarctic and perialpine lakes (Douglas et al. 1999, Østbye et al. 2005, Kahilainen and Østbye 2006, Harrod et al. 2010, Hudson et al. 2011).

Subpopulations inhabiting these systems largely diversified in the wake of the most recent glacial period 10,000-15,000 years ago. They are typified by parallel patterns of divergence in traits associated with foraging (i.e., gill raker counts, benthic vs. pelagic feeding ecology), physiology (i.e., growth rate, habitat depth partitioning) and reproductive ecology (i.e., reproductive timing and spawning habitat).

Up to six different sympatric forms sometimes referred to as “morphs”, "ecomorphs" or "ecotypes" have been recorded in perialpine lakes, and these radiations might be even more diverse in some large systems of northeastern Europe (Præbel et al. 2013, Doenz et al. 2018, Bitz‐Thorsen et al. 2020, Öhlund et al. 2020).

However, there exist significant differences in opinion regarding the taxonomic status of these forms.

In northern Europe, including the United Kingdom, all except a handful of Irish subpopulations are usually regarded as belonging to two widely-distributed species; Coregonus albula (ciscoes) and C. lavaretus (whitefishes), with the latter also frequently referred to as the "Coregonus lavaretus species complex” (Etheridge et al. 2012, Wanke et al. 2017, Häkli et al. 2018, Crotti et al. 2020). Within this comparatively uniform taxonomic concept, the catch-all English vernacular name “Vendace” is typically used for C. albula while "Common Whitefish" or "European Whitefish" are applied to C. lavaretus.

Conversely, researchers and fisheries authorities based in Central Europe have tended to treat the different forms as distinct taxa, leading to the recognition of more than 60 species across the European region (Kottelat and Freyhof 2007, Selz et al. 2020, De-Kayne et al. 2022, Selz and Seehausen 2023). Under this diverse taxonomic concept, the name “Vendace” is restricted to its original usage for the United Kingdom endemic Coregonus vandesius and the native range of C. lavaretus is limited to its type locality of Lake Bourget in France.

With the above in mind, it appears unlikely that the striking phenotypic diversity exhibited by members of this genus will ever be adequately represented by a single accepted taxonomic system. In the absence of a region-wide consensus, the IUCN Red List broadly follows the taxonomy provided by Fricke et al. (2024).
